do: Keep the title inside the category limit (commonly 200 characters, some categories stricter) and front-load brand, product and the deciding attribute.
dont: Do not exceed the limit or pad it with keyword strings; long titles are truncated on mobile and can be suppressed.
why: Mobile search results cut titles early, so anything after the limit never reaches the buyer.
source: Amazon Seller Central - product title requirements (category style guides)

do: Describe the product factually: brand, product name, key attribute, size or count.
dont: Do not use promotional language such as free shipping, best seller, sale, deal, or money-back.
why: Promotional phrases are prohibited in titles and are a common cause of listing suppression.
source: Amazon Seller Central - prohibited seller content

do: Write titles in normal sentence case; capitalise a brand name only if that is the registered form.
dont: Do not set whole words or phrases in ALL CAPS for emphasis.
why: All-caps titles violate style guidance and read as shouting, which lowers click-through.
source: Amazon Seller Central - product title style

do: Follow brand + product + key attribute + size/count, so the buyer can identify the item from the title alone.
dont: Do not produce keyword soup with repeated attributes or unrelated search terms.
why: Buyers scan the first few words; relevance and readability drive click-through more than keyword count.
source: Amazon Seller Central - product title requirements

do: Use every available bullet (usually five) with one distinct benefit each.
dont: Do not leave bullets empty or repeat the same claim in different words.
why: Bullets are the main scan surface on mobile and each unused slot is lost selling space.

do: Keep each bullet to one idea, roughly 150-250 characters, leading with the benefit.
dont: Do not write paragraph-length bullets or bury the benefit after three clauses.
why: Long bullets are collapsed behind 'read more' on mobile and lose the reader.

do: Make only claims the product documentation supports, and keep the evidence on file.
dont: Do not use FDA approved, cures, treats, prevents, or any disease claim on a supplement or food listing.
why: Disease claims are restricted for supplements and are a frequent cause of takedowns.
source: Amazon Seller Central - dietary supplements policy

do: Fill the backend search terms with synonyms and misspellings that are not already in the title, within the byte limit.
dont: Do not repeat title words, include competitor brand names, or exceed the byte limit.
why: Repeats add nothing to indexing and competitor names create policy risk.

do: Use a pure white background (RGB 255,255,255) with the product filling most of the frame.
dont: Do not put lifestyle scenes, props, text or graphics on the main image.
why: The main image has its own policy; violations can hide the listing from search.
source: Amazon Seller Central - product image requirements

do: Upload at least 1000 px on the longest side (1600 px or more for zoom) and keep a square 1:1 frame.
dont: Do not upload low-resolution or stretched images to save space.
why: Below the zoom threshold the buyer cannot inspect the product, which depresses conversion.
source: Amazon Seller Central - product image requirements

do: Show the actual product cleanly; use secondary images for context and scale.
dont: Do not add watermarks, logos, badges or promotional text to product images.
why: Overlays on images are prohibited and make the listing ineligible for some placements.
source: Amazon Seller Central - product image requirements

do: Group the same product in different sizes, colours or counts as one variation family.
dont: Do not mix different products, brands or incompatible categories into one family.
why: Wrong variation families split reviews and can be broken apart by Amazon.

do: Use plain text for the description when the brand has A+ content, and reserve rich layout for A+.
dont: Do not inject HTML, JavaScript, or external links into the description.
why: Unsupported markup is stripped or rejected, and links to external sites are prohibited.

do: Match the condition to the real item state and use the standard condition grades (for example Used - Like New).
dont: Do not list an opened, tested or customer-returned item as New.
why: Condition mismatches drive returns, negative feedback and account health warnings.

do: Keep supplier invoices that match the brand, quantity and date window for gated categories.
dont: Do not submit retail receipts or screenshots as proof of authenticity.
why: Gating reviews reject retail receipts, and a failed review can block the category for the account.
source: Amazon Seller Central - selling approval and invoices

do: Pair structure/function claims with the required disclaimer and keep substantiation on file.
dont: Do not imply the product diagnoses, treats, cures or prevents a disease.
why: Supplements are a restricted category; unsupported claims risk removal and regulatory exposure.
source: Amazon Seller Central - dietary supplements policy

do: Lead the title with the brand, then the product and the deciding attribute
dont: Bury the brand after a keyword string
why: Buyers scan brand and product first, and the first words decide the click
source: Amazon Seller Central - product title requirements

do: Open each bullet with the benefit, then the feature that proves it
dont: Open with a raw specification and hope the buyer infers the benefit
why: Mobile shoppers scan the first three words of each bullet

do: Use image two for scale or the product in use
dont: Repeat the main image or spend the slot on a logo
why: The second image answers the objection the first one created

do: Describe value with facts the buyer can verify
dont: Claim cheapest or best value in the listing copy
why: Unverifiable superlatives are a policy risk and erode trust

do: Choose the most specific browse node the product actually fits
dont: Pick the largest top-level category for reach
why: Wrong nodes hide the product from category browsing

do: Keep the parent as the family and every child as one real variant
dont: Attach unrelated ASINs to consolidate reviews
why: Wrong variation families get split by Amazon and lose the review pool

do: Put the strongest visual claim in the first A+ module
dont: Open A+ with a logo or a wall of badges
why: The first screen decides whether the buyer scrolls
